question: You notice a colleague at work with tears in his eyes during a crucial project deadline. Describe how you would balance your immediate task responsibilities with responding to your colleague's emotional state.
answer:
I see my colleague struggling, and honestly, it tugs at me. Work deadlines matter, but that person matters too—and pretending I didn't notice would feel wrong.

Here's what I'd do: I'd gently check in first. Maybe walk over, lower my voice, and ask something simple like, "Hey, everything okay? I've got a minute if you need to talk." Sometimes people just need a moment to feel seen. I'd give them space to share or not share—whichever they need.

Then I'd look for a practical balance. If it's a quick breakdown, maybe I can help shoulder some of their workload temporarily. Or I could grab them a coffee and suggest they take five minutes to breathe while I cover something small on their plate. The deadline doesn't disappear, but human support can sometimes help someone push through rather than completely shut down.

If things are more serious or need longer, I'd offer to flag it with our manager—that we're both feeling the pressure and might need a brief pause. Good managers understand that burnt-out people make more mistakes anyway.

I wouldn't ignore the elephant in the room to protect my own tasks. That feels cold. At the same time, I'd be honest with myself about my own limits—I can't solve everything, and taking on too much helps nobody.

Ultimately, I'd trust my gut. If my colleague needs me urgently, I'll make it work. If they wave me off, I'll check back later. Small gestures—a kind word, a helping hand—often matter more than any single deadline.

Work is important, but we're humans first. I can always hustle to meet a deadline. I can't get back a moment where I chose productivity over compassion.

When she apologized, I'd probably just say something like, "Hey, it's okay. I know you didn't mean to. I'm just frustrated about missing the event, but I'm not upset with you." I'd want to reassure her that our friendship matters more than one mistake.

Maybe I'd also laugh a little and say something like, "Next time, though, maybe set five alarms—or better yet, give me a call at 6 AM so I can be sure!" Humor helps ease the tension and reminds us both that this isn't worth dwelling on.

I'd probably ask her what happened—maybe she overslept too, or had an emergency—and just listen. I don't want to make her feel worse than she already does. Apologizing takes courage, and I respect that she owned up to it instead of making excuses.

At the end of the day, true friendship means forgiving the small stuff and showing up for each other anyway. Yeah, I'm disappointed about the event, but I'd rather have my friend feeling okay than guilty. Life's too short to hold grudges over honest mistakes.

answer:

Changing plans isn't a big deal in the grand scheme, and I'd want them to do the same for me. Friendship means being flexible sometimes.

But I'd be lying if I said I never felt that little twinge of hesitation. Maybe I had something I was looking forward to, or I was tired and was planning a quiet night in. That stuff matters too.

What I'd probably do is pause for a second, maybe check in with myself about what I actually have going on. If it's nothing urgent on my end, I usually just say yes. If it's something I really committed to—like tickets to something or I promised someone else—I'd be honest about that. "I totally want to help, but I already told my sister I'd be there" or whatever.

I think there's this balance between being a good friend and not becoming a pushover who never does anything for themselves. The agreeable part of me wants to just say yes and figure it out, but the part that's learned to respect my own boundaries knows that's not sustainable.

Mostly, I'd just be real with them about it. Most friends get it. The ones who get upset just because you can't rearrange your whole life? Those relationships get exhausting.

So yeah—my gut answer is usually yes, but with some honest checking in first.

I'd probably glance at my watch first—I'm human, after all—and weigh the options. But honestly? A few extra minutes wouldn't ruin my day. The meeting will understand if I'm a little late, and that stranger's relief would be worth so much more to me.

I'd approach them with a friendly smile and just ask if they need a hand. Sometimes people are too proud or surprised to accept help, but most folks light up when someone notices them. I'd offer to carry a bag or two, maybe walk with them if they're heading my direction. Even if not, a few steps of assistance makes a difference.

What gets me is the simple humanity of it. We're all just people navigating our days, carrying our own burdens—sometimes literally. That moment of connection, where someone acknowledges you're struggling and steps up? It means everything.

I don't think I'd feel guilty for stopping. If anything, I'd feel lighter. There's something genuinely rewarding about helping, even in small ways. It grounds me and reminds me that my to-do list isn't the center of the universe.

So yes, strong urge. Almost automatic. I'd help.

question: You are running late for an important meeting. As you walk down the street, you notice someone drop his wallet. What do you do next?
answer:

Instinctively I slow down, then stop. “Hey, excuse me! You dropped your wallet!” I call out, trying not to sound as breathless as I feel.

He turns, eyes wide, and I see the relief flood his face. I bend down, pick it up, and hand it over. He fumbles for his phone, checks the cash, and says, “Thank you, man, I didn’t even realize.” I smile, “No worries, just be careful.”

Inside, I’m torn: the meeting’s starting in ten minutes and I’m still a block away. I glance at my watch, then at the guy, and decide that a few extra seconds of honesty is worth more than a punctual excuse. I call my boss, “Hey, I’m running a couple minutes late, I stopped to help someone who dropped their wallet.” He sounds understanding, tells me to take my time.

After the quick exchange, I jog the rest of the way, feeling a strange mix of urgency and calm. The meeting’s first slide is already up when I slip in, but the brief apology I make feels sincere. Later, I realize that while I was late, the moment of helping someone else made the whole morning feel less frantic. It’s a reminder that sometimes the small, kind actions ground us, even when we’re chasing the next big thing. I’m glad I didn’t just keep walking.

Can I share my concerns?" I'd try to keep my tone curious rather than confrontational, because I'm genuinely asking, not telling them they're wrong.

I might then briefly explain what I'm seeing differently—maybe a risk they haven't considered, or an angle I think we're overlooking. But I'd also make clear I could be missing context or that I respect their expertise in areas where they know more than me.

If they still feel confident after I've spoken, I'd probably go along with the decision, at least for now. Being agreeable doesn't mean being a pushover, but it does mean I value team cohesion and trust. I'd rather support a decision I have reservations about than create unnecessary conflict—unless, of course, the consequences of going along would be serious. In that case, I'd quietly flag my concerns afterward to a manager or trusted colleague.

Honestly, it feels uncomfortable in the moment, but I think that's normal. Good teams aren't the ones where everyone agrees—they're the ones where people feel safe voicing concerns and being heard.

question: Imagine you are leading a team project and one of your team members, who has been consistently contributing well, suddenly starts struggling with her tasks. How would you approach this team member about her performance issues?
